reason: Đoạn Standard Levenshtein distance permits three elementary edit operations. Phân biệt mô hình cụ thể với họ edit distance; phối hợp sửa định nghĩa trang chủ.
source_excerpt: Standard Levenshtein distance permits three elementary edit operations: Operation Meaning Example Standard Cost Insertion Add one sequence element ct → cat 1 Deletion Remove one sequence element cart → cat 1 Substitution Replace one sequence element cat → cut 1 Matching equal sequence elements has zero cost. insert = 1 delete = 1 substitute = 1 match = 0 Under this model, Levenshtein distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform one sequence into another. See Edit Operations & Edit Scripts .

source_excerpt: Approximate string matching is especially useful when differences are primarily local changes in symbolic sequences. Typical applications include: spelling correction, noisy user queries, OCR post-correction, name and address matching, record linkage, identifier comparison, approximate dictionary lookup, selected biological sequence tasks. It becomes less appropriate when the dominant difference involves meaning, large structural changes, word reordering, or relationships not well modeled by sequence edits.

source_excerpt: No. Approximate edit distance asks: approximately compute ED(x,y) for a given pair. Approximate string matching asks: find substrings / records whose distance from a pattern is sufficiently small The latter contains an indexing or search problem in addition to pairwise distance computation.

source_excerpt: Robert A. Wagner and Michael J. Fischer published The String-to-String Correction Problem in the Journal of the ACM in January 1974. The paper formalized the problem as finding a minimum-cost sequence of single-symbol changes, deletions, and insertions and presented an algorithm whose running time is proportional to the product of the two string lengths. The authors identified automatic spelling correction and longest-common-subsequence computation among the applications of the framework. The algorithm became one of the foundational dynamic-programming formulations in string algorithms and remains a reference point for subsequent work on approximate matching, bounded edit distance, sequence comparison, alignment, and optimized Levenshtein computation.

reason: The historical result: tên Algorithms for Approximate String Matching có sẵn; giữ DOI ngoài.
source_excerpt: In his 1985 paper Algorithms for Approximate String Matching , Esko Ukkonen started from the classical tabulation method and developed improved algorithms whose running time depends on the actual edit distance s . For strings of lengths m and n , the paper gives an algorithm with: Time: O(s · min(m,n)) Space: O(s · min(m,n)) and discusses improved space bounds. In the special case where edit operations have character-independent equal costs, Ukkonen gives an algorithm with: Time: O(s · min(m,n)) Space: O(s · min(s,m,n)) When the actual editing sequence is not required, the algorithms can be implemented with space: O(min(s,m,n)) The same work also derives a threshold decision procedure: given a threshold t , determine whether: d(x,y) ≤ t in: Time: O(t · min(m,n)) Space: O(min(t,m,n)) These bounds make the algorithm output-sensitive : performance improves when the resulting distance is small.

source_excerpt: Bit-parallel approximate matching predates Myers' 1999 paper. Earlier methods, including work by Wu and Manber, represented active states of approximate-matching automata with bit vectors. Myers introduced a different representation based directly on the dynamic-programming matrix's horizontal and vertical differences. Because those differences are restricted to -1 , 0 , and +1 , a whole column of DP state can be encoded using positive and negative bit masks. The paper's crucial technical step is the derivation of a constant-size word-operation sequence for advancing this representation, including the integer-addition carry-propagation formula for Xh . The result was published as A Fast Bit-Vector Algorithm for Approximate String Matching Based on Dynamic Programming in the Journal of the ACM , volume 46, issue 3, pages 395–415, in May 1999.

source_excerpt: Klaus U. Schulz and Stoyan Mihov developed a highly influential deterministic construction for Levenshtein automata. For any fixed distance bound: k and pattern: P their method can construct a deterministic Levenshtein automaton in time linear in: |P| with the constant depending on the fixed degree k . This is a central theoretical and practical result because it means the deterministic machine does not need to be obtained by performing an unrestricted generic powerset construction for every word.

source_excerpt: Arturs Backurs and Piotr Indyk established one of the foundational results in fine-grained complexity for edit distance. They showed that an algorithm computing exact edit distance in: O( n^(2-δ) ) for any constant: δ > 0 would imply a faster SAT algorithm contradicting SETH. Thus, assuming SETH: no exact strongly subquadratic edit-distance algorithm exists

source_excerpt: Let the reference transcription be the word sequence R = (r1, r2, ..., rN) and the ASR hypothesis be H = (h1, h2, ..., hM). After aligning the two sequences, let: S = number of substitutions; D = number of deletions; I = number of insertions; C = number of correctly matched reference words; N = number of words in the reference. Since every reference word is either correct, substituted, or deleted, N = C + S + D. The conventional word error rate is S + D + I WER = ------------------------- N or, as a percentage, S + D + I WER (%) = 100 * --------------- N The definition corresponds to a word-level form of Levenshtein distance : instead of comparing individual characters, the atomic symbols are words. This relationship is fundamental but should not be overstated. WER is a task-specific evaluation statistic built from edit operations. It is not merely another name for Levenshtein distance because WER adds a particular denominator, a transcription protocol, and often scorer-specific alignment rules.

source_excerpt: Fault-tolerant search Fault-tolerant search Classical approaches to error-tolerant search This is a brief description of the most relevant "classical" approaches to tackle the problem of error-tolerant search. Deterministic Finite Automat on (DFA or Transducer) DFAs are based on regular languages, widely used in compilers and interpreters to quickly check words for membership in a defined word set. The retrieval in this kind of structure is based on a directed walk through a set of states. This is usually extremely fast and independent of the size of the dictionary. Error tolerance can only be added by either considering expected variations of the query string or by adding such to the dictionary. This ends up being a trial-and-error approach, which is naturally very limited. In the former case the retrieval time grows exponentially with the number of allowed errors and the latter is not manageable in terms of memory consumption for large dictionaries. In general this approach is maximally good for up to 2 corrections. The major drawback of this approach is that resource consumption increases exponentially with the number of corrections. Hash Tables There are a wide range of implementations of hash tables. All of them have the advantage that the procedure is extremely fast (constant), but not fault tolerant at all. Error-tolerance is usually applied by doubling the hash table and by accessing it with the so-called "front hash"-"back hash" procedure, assuming that an error occurs only in one half of the word. Memory resources are comparably small. There are implementations which have a built-in hash for special situations, where time can be saved when a perfect match is sufficient. There is no commercially available solution that relies on this technology. Associative Mem
